title: Brewster's Law and Polarization by Reflection
short_intro: Brewster's law states that when unpolarized light is incident on a transparent dielectric surface at a specific angle called the polarizing angle, the reflected light is completely plane-polarized. At this angle of incidence, the reflected and refracted rays are mutually perpendicular to each other.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of polarizing angle (Brewster angle), statement of Brewster's law, relation between refractive index and tangent of Brewster angle (mu = tan i_p), and the perpendicularity condition between reflected and refracted rays.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Vector formulation of reflection and refraction, phase changes upon reflection at dielectric boundaries, derivation from electromagnetic boundary conditions (Fresnel equations), and behavior of multi-plate glass stacks for polarization.

prerequisites: Wave nature of light and transverse nature of electromagnetic waves
Concept of plane-polarized and unpolarized light

concept_notes.heading: Polarization by Reflection
bullets: When an unpolarized light beam strikes a smooth interface separating two transparent dielectric media, both reflection and refraction occur.
The reflected beam is partially polarized for all angles of incidence except one specific angle known as the polarizing angle or Brewster's angle (i_p).

At the polarizing angle, the electric field vector oscillating parallel to the plane of incidence is completely transmitted, leaving the reflected ray entirely polarized with vibrations perpendicular to the plane of incidence.

concept_notes.heading: Brewster's Law Formulation
bullets: Sir David Brewster discovered experimentally in 1812 that the tangent of the polarizing angle of incidence equals the refractive index of the denser medium with respect to the rarer medium.
Mathematically expressed as tan(i_p) = mu_21, where mu_21 is the refractive index of medium 2 with respect to medium 1.
When light travels from air or vacuum (mu = 1) into a medium of refractive index mu, the relation simplifies to tan(i_p) = mu.

concept_notes.heading: Geometric Condition at Brewster Angle
bullets: At the polarizing angle of incidence i_p, the angle between the reflected ray and the refracted ray is exactly 90 degrees.
Using Snell's law (sin i_p / sin r = mu) and Brewster's law (mu = sin i_p / cos i_p), it follows that sin i_p / sin r = sin i_p / cos i_p.
This implies sin r = cos i_p = sin(90 - i_p), leading to r = 90 - i_p, or i_p + r = 90 degrees.

concept_notes.heading: Degree of Polarization and Intensity
bullets: The reflected intensity is a fraction of the incident unpolarized intensity, and at Brewster's angle, it consists solely of light polarized perpendicular to the plane of incidence.
Brewster's windows are used in lasers to minimize reflection losses for the polarization parallel to the plane of incidence.
Polarization by reflection is independent of the wavelength of light, except for minor variations in refractive index due to dispersion.

derivations.title: Derivation of Brewster's Law from Snell's Law
derivations.conditions: Light incident from a medium of refractive index mu_1 to a medium of refractive index mu_2 at polarizing angle i_p.
steps: Apply Snell's law at the interface: mu_1 sin i_p = mu_2 sin r, where i_p is the polarizing angle and r is the angle of refraction.
State the geometric condition at Brewster's angle: the reflected ray and refracted ray are perpendicular, meaning i_p + r = 90 degrees, or r = 90 - i_p.
Substitute r into Snell's law: mu_1 sin i_p = mu_2 sin(90 - i_p) = mu_2 cos i_p.
Rearrange the terms to find the ratio of sine and cosine: sin i_p / cos i_p = mu_2 / mu_1.
Express as tangent: tan i_p = mu_2 / mu_1 = mu_21.

derivations.title: Reflected and Refracted Ray Perpendicularity Derivation
derivations.conditions: Plane interface between two dielectric media satisfying Brewster's law.
steps: Let i_p be the angle of incidence equal to Brewster's angle, and r be the angle of refraction.
From Brewster's law, tan i_p = mu_2 / mu_1 = sin i_p / cos i_p.
From Snell's law, mu_2 / mu_1 = sin i_p / sin r.
Equating the two expressions gives sin i_p / cos i_p = sin i_p / sin r.
Canceling sin i_p yields cos i_p = sin r = cos(90 - r), which means i_p = 90 - r or i_p + r = 90 degrees.

Since the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence (i_p), the angle between the reflected ray (at angle i_p to the normal) and the refracted ray (at angle r to the normal) is 180 - (i_p + r) = 180 - 90 = 90 degrees.
derivations.result: Angle between reflected and refracted rays = 90 degrees

graphs_and_experiments.title: Intensity vs Angle of Incidence Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot showing reflected light intensity (I_p for parallel polarization and I_s for perpendicular polarization) against the angle of incidence i. I_p drops to zero at i = i_p.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: At Brewster's angle i_p, the component of light polarized parallel to the plane of incidence has zero reflection coefficient. Only the perpendicular component is reflected.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct identification of Brewster's angle from polarization curves in multi-choice questions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Reflection and Refraction Setup at Brewster Angle
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A ray diagram showing an unpolarized incident ray hitting a glass slab at angle i_p, a completely polarized reflected ray at angle i_p, and a mutually perpendicular refracted ray at angle r.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the 90-degree spatial separation between the reflected and refracted rays, confirming the geometric foundation of Brewster's law.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical problem visualization and conceptual ray tracing.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Pile of Plates Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Several parallel glass plates arranged such that unpolarized light is incident at Brewster's angle, producing a transmitted beam that is strongly polarized parallel to the plane of incidence.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Successive reflections remove the perpendicular polarization component, polarizing the transmitted beam through multiple partial reflections.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual questions on generating polarized light without polaroids.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the polarizing angle for glass of refractive index 1.5. (Given tan(56.3 degrees) = 1.5)
solution_steps: Identify the given refractive index: mu = 1.5.
Use Brewster's law formula: tan(i_p) = mu.
Find the inverse tangent: i_p = arctan(1.5) = 56.3 degrees.

solved_numericals.question: Light is incident from air onto a water surface of refractive index 4/3 at the polarizing angle. Find the angle of refraction.
solution_steps: State the relationship at the polarizing angle for air-water interface: i_p + r = 90 degrees.
Find the polarizing angle: i_p = arctan(4/3) = arctan(1.333) approx 53.13 degrees.
Calculate the angle of refraction r: r = 90 degrees - 53.13 degrees.

solved_numericals.question: The angle between the reflected and refracted rays of light when incident on a transparent medium is 90 degrees. If the angle of refraction is 30 degrees, find the refractive index of the medium.
solution_steps: Given that the angle between reflected and refracted rays is 90 degrees, the incidence angle i_p satisfies the Brewster condition: i_p + r = 90 degrees.
Given angle of refraction r = 30 degrees.
Calculate incidence angle i_p: i_p = 90 degrees - 30 degrees = 60 degrees.
Apply Brewster's law to find refractive index: mu = tan(i_p) = tan(60 degrees).

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes the media are optically isotropic, non-magnetic (relative permeability mu_r approx 1), and transparent dielectrics.
Does not hold strictly for absorbing media (metals), where the refractive index is complex and minimum reflection does not yield complete polarization.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The reflected light is partially polarized only at angles greater than Brewster's angle.
common_misconceptions.correct: The reflected light is partially polarized at all angles of incidence except normal incidence, but it is 100% plane-polarized exclusively at Brewster's angle.
common_misconceptions.why: Polarization degree varies continuously with angle, peaking at i_p.

common_misconceptions.wrong: At Brewster's angle, both the reflected and refracted rays are completely polarized.
common_misconceptions.correct: Only the reflected ray is completely polarized. The refracted ray remains partially polarized because it contains a mixture of both parallel and perpendicular polarization components.
common_misconceptions.why: Refraction transmits some of both orthogonal electric field components.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Brewster's law applies only when light travels from air to a denser medium.
common_misconceptions.correct: Brewster's law is valid for light passing between any two transparent dielectric media, where tan(i_p) = mu_2 / mu_1.
common_misconceptions.why: The relative refractive index governs the relation regardless of whether mu_1 is unity.

quick_revision: Brewster's law formula is tan(i_p) = mu_2 / mu_1, defining the angle where reflected light is completely plane-polarized.
Brewster's Law for Air-Medium Interface: tan(i_p) = \mu
